title: Quick-Number Intake
description: The 60-second intake question(s) every DA should ask before firing a SQL query. The discipline is asking once before answering — not every time, just every time the request is ambiguous enough that the answer could be wrong. This template is for the DA; it never gets sent to the stakeholder.
empty_template_md:
# Quick-Number Intake — Internal Template
_For the DA's use, not the stakeholder's. Run through before any 'quick number' request._

## 1. What decision will this number inform?
_If the answer is 'I just want to know', the number doesn't matter and we can hand them anything. Usually the answer is more specific._

## 2. By when do they need it?
_'EOD', 'before my 5pm meeting', 'this week'. The time window shapes how much intake conversation is appropriate._

## 3. What's the most likely intended cut?
_The default interpretation of the request. Send this as the answer with the alternatives one-line below — gives the stakeholder a fast-path to confirm or correct._

## 4. Where could the answer be wrong?
_What's the most likely data quality / definition / time-window gotcha. Two minutes thinking here saves 24 hours of post-hoc embarrassment._

## 5. Could the answer be ambiguous in a way that matters?
_If 'customer signups' could mean gross-vs-net-vs-paid-vs-trial, the right response includes the most likely cut PLUS one-line alternatives. If it can only mean one thing, don't waste the stakeholder's time on intake._

## 6. Send template
_How to phrase the answer when sending. The 'lead with the most likely answer, list the alternatives in one line, offer the door open' format is the working default._

worked_examples.title: Bilqis's 'how many customers signed up last month' — the 90-second intake
worked_examples.content_md:
# Quick-Number Intake — Bilqis's Signups Question

_Request received: 16.55, Tuesday 22 April. Bilqis going into a meeting at 17.00._
_Intake time available: ~60 seconds before responding._

## 1. What decision will this inform?

She's quoting it in a meeting that starts in 5 minutes. The decision context is whatever's in that meeting — probably commercial / board / strategy. The number needs to be defensible if questioned, but doesn't need a full caveat list. She'll use it directionally, but cite it specifically.

## 2. By when?

2-3 minutes. After that, she walks in without the number.

## 3. Most likely intended cut

**Net new paid customers in March 2026.** That's the most common version of 'signups' that someone at her level would quote — the one finance reports against and that maps to revenue conversation. 'Customers' usually means paid, not trial. 'Last month' on 22 April means March, the most recently closed reporting month.

## 4. Where could the answer be wrong?

- **Partner-channel triple-count incident (18-25 March):** the raw signups table has duplicate rows from that pipeline issue. If I run a naive `count(*)`, I overcount by ~3,127.
- **Trial-vs-paid:** if I count all signups, I'll send ~840 including trials, but she probably wants paid (~412). 2× difference depending on interpretation.
- **Net-of-churn:** finance sometimes reports net-of-churn (additions minus losses, ~390). Likely a smaller question, but possible.

## 5. Could it be ambiguous?

Yes — three plausible cuts (paid gross, all signups, net-of-churn) within ~2× of each other. The intake question takes 30 seconds to answer; she'll prefer that to a wrong number quoted to the board.

## 6. The send

> 'Net new paid in March — 412. Happy to swap to inc. trials (~840) or net-of-churn (~390) if useful — let me know which works.'

Three sentences. Specific number lead. Alternatives in one line. Door open. She replies in 90 seconds: 'net new paid is fine, thanks!' and walks into the meeting.

annotations.note: Decision-context — even guessed — shapes the response. A board-level quote needs more defensiveness than a 'just curious' question. The DA who never asks 'what is this for' often ends up answering the wrong question well.
Lead with the most-likely cut — don't open with 'which cut do you want?' The stakeholder usually doesn't know what cuts exist; offering one is more useful than asking them to specify.
The data-quality knowns are what saves the DA from sending a 60%-wrong number. The 90 seconds you spend reviewing what could be wrong is the most valuable 90 seconds in the whole interaction.
Three-sentence response: specific number with the cut named, alternatives in one line, door open. Format is consistent enough that stakeholders learn to scan it; they reply 'X is fine' in 30 seconds.

common_mistakes: Skipping intake on 'easy' requests. Most ambiguous requests look easy on the surface ('how many customers signed up?').
Asking the intake question OF the stakeholder when you could answer it yourself. 'What do you mean by customer?' is a worse response than 'Net new paid: 412; alternatives are X, Y'.
Sending the most defensive answer (full caveats, methodology, footnotes). Defensive answers are useless when the stakeholder has 90 seconds.
Sending the wrong cut without naming it. The number is wrong, the stakeholder quotes it, and the DA's credibility takes the hit.
Treating every quick-number request as needing a one-page brief. Sometimes 'X' is the right answer. The DA's job is to know which is which.
Not learning the data quality knowns. The triple-count incident is a real example; without knowing it, you'd send the wrong number from a naive query.
variant_patterns: High-context-stakeholder variant: a stakeholder you've worked with for months may know the cuts already. Send the number with one-line context, not the full alternatives list.
First-time-stakeholder variant: spend extra intake time on §1 (decision context). You don't yet know what they'll do with the number.
Compliance-sensitive variant: any number going into a regulated submission requires full caveat tracking. The 60-second intake doesn't apply; switch to the full stakeholder-summary playbook.
